Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX) IPO Process: A Practical Research Report

Listing eligibility, review procedures, key deadlines and practical considerations for the Main Board and GEM. Information current as of 26 November 2026. The rule basis is the Main Board Listing Rules and GEM Listing Rules currently in force, together with public documents of HKEX and the SFC. 1. Executive Summary This report sets out the complete initial public offering (IPO) process on the Main Board and GEM of Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX), focusing on three questions: who can list, who does the work, and in what sequence and over what timeframe. All rule references are drawn from the Main Board Listing Rules and GEM Listing Rules currently in force and from public documents of HKEX and the SFC, with a clause index and sources listed in the appendices. 1.1 Five Key Conclusions ① Dual-track regulation. The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong (SEHK, an HKEX subsidiary) reviews listing eligibility and rule compliance; the SFC concurrently reviews disclosure through “dual filing” and may object to an application or impose conditions; the prospectus must also be registered under the Companies (Winding Up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance (Cap. 32). ② Four hard deadlines. An A1 may be filed only after the sponsor has been formally appointed for a full 2 months; an A1 remains valid for 6 months; the prospectus must be substantially finalised 4 “full business days” before the hearing; a returned application may be resubmitted only after 8 weeks. ③ Three financial tests on the Main Board. Profit test; market capitalisation/revenue/cash flow test; market capitalisation/revenue test. Pre-revenue biotech and Specialist Technology companies may follow Chapter 18A and Chapter 18C respectively. ④ Typical timeline. About 8–15 months from formal sponsor appointment to listing, and about 6–12 months from A1 submission. These are market experience figures; the rules themselves set only caps and checkpoints, not committed timelines. ⑤ Recent changes. From August 2025 public float follows a new market-cap-tiered scale; FINI has compressed IPO settlement to T+2; the market-wide T+1 target is the second half of 2028. 1.2 Scope and Methodology Basis: HKEX’s electronic Main Board Listing Rules (including Chapters 3A, 8, 9, 11A, 12, 18A and 18C), Chapter 11 of the GEM Listing Rules, the Main Board Fees Rules, Practice Notes PN18/PN22, the SFC dual filing page and HKEX market information pages. Conventions: unless otherwise stated, all amounts are in Hong Kong dollars; “typical duration” and “usual practice” reflect market experience and are not rule commitments; rule provisions are governed by the English text, and the Chinese wording is a paraphrase for readability. As at: information is current as of 26 November 2026. Rules are amended frequently, and live transactions should rely on the version in force at the time of submission. 2. The Hong Kong IPO Market and Listing Architecture 2.1 Market Position Hong Kong is one of the world’s leading equity fundraising markets. According to HKEX, Hong Kong ranked first globally by IPO proceeds in 2025, raising more than US$36 billion over the year; since the new economy listing regime was introduced in 2018, more than 430 new economy companies have listed in Hong Kong, raising over US$150 billion in aggregate. As at 2025, around 167 biotech companies had listed under Chapter 18A. The direct implication for issuers is that the Hong Kong market provides two sources of capital—international institutional money and Mainland Chinese money (through the mutual access mechanisms)—and has dedicated channels for weighted voting rights, pre-revenue biotech, Specialist Technology, SPACs and other special structures, giving issuers considerable choice of board. 2.2 Listing Architecture and Boards Table 1 HKEX Listing Boards and Special Channels Board / Chapter Positioning Core features Main Board For mature companies with a certain scale and profit/revenue track record Three financial tests; Listing Eligibility and Board Selection 3.1 The Three Financial Tests on the Main Board A Main Board applicant must satisfy one of three tests (Rule 8.05). The “soft” conditions common to all three are a trading record of not less than three financial years, management continuity over the three most recent financial years, and ownership continuity over the most recent audited financial year. Large revenue but thin profit: assess the market cap/revenue test first; where operating cash flow is sound, the market cap/revenue/cash flow test requires a lower market cap threshold (HK$2 billion versus HK$4 billion). Pre-revenue biotech: Chapter 18A; the R&D progress of core products and sophisticated investors are the focus of review. Specialist Technology (including AI, robotics and new materials): Chapter 18C; first determine whether the company is “commercialised” or “pre-commercial”—there is a HK$4 billion gap between the two market cap thresholds. Small and medium-sized enterprises: GEM has lower thresholds, and of the two tests the cash flow test imposes no hard profit requirement, suiting companies with steady operating cash flow. 4. The core task is not “writing materials” but turning the company into an entity that the capital markets can understand and the regulators can accept. Determining the board and test path: first run market cap and financial projections, then work backwards to identify the applicable test; where the profit test applies, ensure that profit in the most recent year and the two preceding years all meet the thresholds, excluding one-off gains. Restructuring: choosing a red-chip / H-share / VIE structure; establishing a Cayman or BVI holding platform; injecting domestic interests; unwinding nominee shareholdings; regularising employee shareholding platforms. Independence and competing business: where a controlling shareholder operates a competing business, the listing document must make full disclosure under Rule 8.10 and demonstrate that the applicant can operate independently; connected transactions must be eliminated or regularised. Pre-IPO investment: the timing, valuation and special rights of investors (repurchase, liquidation preference, etc.) must be properly addressed before submission and are usually required to be terminated or adjusted before listing. Financials and internal controls: preparing three-year (Main Board) or two-year (GEM) statements under the applicable accounting standards (HKFRS/IFRS); revenue recognition, customer concentration and related-party fund flows are frequently queried. Compliance review: licences, environmental protection, work safety, labour and social security, tax, data and cybersecurity, and intellectual property. 5.3 Stage 2: Sponsor Appointment and Due Diligence The sponsor must be engaged under a written engagement letter and must notify SEHK in writing as soon as practicable after appointment. The key hard rule is that a listing application may not be submitted less than 2 months after the date of the sponsor’s formal appointment; where there are multiple sponsors, the clock runs from the formal appointment of the last sponsor (Rule 3A.02B). In practice this rule makes “finding a sponsor” the starting point of the project timetable. The sponsor must conduct reasonable due diligence in accordance with Practice Note 21 (PN21) and bears statutory responsibility for material matters in the listing document. In practice the sponsor drives a closed loop of “due diligence checklist—management interviews—third-party verification—working paper archiving” while coordinating lawyers, accountants, valuers and internal control advisers. 5.4 Stage 3: A1 Submission and Dual Filing The applicant files its listing application on Form A1, completed and signed by the sponsor on its behalf, accompanied by the documents specified in Rule 9.10A(1), the Application Proof (the draft listing document) and the initial listing fee. The rules expressly require the application to be “substantially complete”; otherwise SEHK will return the application, return the documents and deal with fees already paid in accordance with the rules; a returned application may be resubmitted no earlier than 8 weeks after the date of return (Rule 9.03(3)). There are two points on publication: first, publication of the Application Proof is “optional”—where the applicant elects to publish, it must submit the Public AP for publication on the same day it files its application with SEHK (Rule 12.01A, PN22); second, whether or not the AP is published, the application must be dual-filed with the SFC through SEHK, and the SFC may object to the application or impose conditions under section 6 of the Securities and Futures (Stock Market Listing) Rules. The initial listing fee is charged by tier according to the monetary value of the securities to be listed and must be paid in advance at the time of application (see Chapter 7). 5.5 Stage 4: Regulatory Review and Enquiries Review is conducted concurrently by the SEHK Listing Division and the SFC, typically in the form of multiple rounds of written enquiries (market experience suggests 3–6 rounds, depending on project complexity). The issuer and sponsor must respond round by round and submit a revised listing document. The rules require that revisions not be “fragmented” and that each version fully address all comments on the previous version (Rule 9.03(5)); the applicant must update SEHK on the progress of its application every two weeks (Rule 9.03(2)). There are two hard timing checkpoints: Six-month validity: if listing is not completed within 6 months from the date of A1 submission, the application lapses and the initial listing fee is not refunded; to continue, a fresh application must be filed and the fee paid again (note 2 to Rule 9.03(1)). Four full business days before the hearing: SEHK may require the hearing to be postponed unless, at least 4 full business days before the hearing, the applicant has submitted a revised listing document containing full disclosure and all outstanding documents, and has satisfactorily resolved the regulatory comments (Rule 9.03(4)). Review focus is not only whether “the numbers add up” but also whether “the business is real, sustainable and suitable for listing”. Common lines of enquiry are set out in Chapter 9. 5.6 Stage 5: Listing Committee Hearing The Listing Committee reviews the application at the hearing and decides to approve, give conditional approval, defer consideration or reject. Before the hearing, the sponsor must ensure that the listing document is final, that all waiver applications (if any) have been submitted and that directors and senior management have completed the necessary declarations. If the application is rejected or approved with conditions, the applicant may apply for a review within the prescribed period, which is considered by the Listing Review Committee. Review is a remedial procedure and should not form part of the normal timetable. 5.7 Stage 6: Post-Hearing Launch and Listing Once the hearing is passed, the project enters the launch execution phase, with the pace driven by the market window. Publication of the PHIP: after receiving the “post-hearing letter” from SEHK and confirming that the principal comments have been addressed, the applicant must publish the Post Hearing Information Pack on the HKEX website as soon as practicable; this is mandatory (Rule 12.01B, PN22). Finalising and registering the prospectus: the prospectus must comply with the Listing Rules and may be issued only after registration with the Companies Registry under the Companies (Winding Up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance (Rule 11A.01). It may not be issued before SEHK confirms that it has no further comments on the listing document (Rule 9.07). Roadshow and bookbuilding: management roadshow, pre-deal analyst discussions and institutional price discovery; the OC coordinates the order book. Public offer and placing: the public offer portion typically accounts for about 10% of the global offering (subject to upward adjustment on clawback), with the placing accounting for the balance; the public offer is divided by application amount into Pool A (HK$5 million and below) and Pool B (above HK$5 million), with the two pools allocated equally (PN18). Where over-subscription reaches the agreed multiples, clawback applies in accordance with the mechanism disclosed in the prospectus. Pricing, allotment and settlement: allocation is determined after pricing and the allotment results are announced; the FINI platform handles subscription monies and share settlement, and the IPO settlement cycle has been shortened from T+5 to T+2. Listing: trading in the shares begins on SEHK; during the stabilisation period (typically 30 days) the over-allotment option (greenshoe, up to 15%) may be exercised; controlling shareholders must comply with lock-up undertakings. 6. Putting these checkpoints together, a reasonably smooth project roughly follows this rhythm (experience-based): T-12 to T-6 months: restructuring, audit, internal control remediation and engaging intermediaries. T-2 months: formal sponsor appointment (no A1 submission before this point). T0: A1 submission, same-day (optional) AP publication, dual filing. T+1 to T+5 months: multiple enquiry rounds and listing document revisions; where financial information is approaching the 6-month validity limit, consider a stub-period audit. T+5 to T+6 months: hearing, PHIP, registration, roadshow and pricing, launch. Around T+6 months: listing. Where there are many enquiry rounds or additional audit is needed, slippage to 9–12 months overall is common. It should be emphasised that the 6-month validity of the A1 is a “countdown”, not a “target”. Once a stub-period audit or slow enquiries make completion within 6 months impossible, the project must be resubmitted with the fee paid again, significantly increasing the time cost. 7. Offering and Pricing Mechanisms 8.1 Offering Structure Public offer: aimed at retail investors, typically 10% of the global offering initially; over-subscription triggers the clawback mechanism, with the clawback percentage applied according to the tiered scale disclosed in the prospectus (commonly 15x, 50x and 100x tiers). Placing: aimed at institutional and professional investors, coordinated by the OC through bookbuilding; the placing portion typically accounts for 90%. Pool A/Pool B: the public offer portion is divided equally into two pools, with Pool A for applicants applying for HK$5 million or less and Pool B for those applying for more than HK$5 million; where one pool is under-subscribed, the surplus is transferred to the other pool (PN18). Cornerstone investors: institutional investors that commit to subscribe before listing, usually subject to a 6-month lock-up; an excessively high cornerstone allocation squeezes the public offer portion and must be disclosed in the prospectus. Over-allotment option (greenshoe): underwriters may over-allot up to 15% of the shares during the stabilisation period to dampen post-listing volatility. 8.2 Settlement and Clearing FINI (Fast Interface for New Issuance) is HKEX’s IPO settlement platform, launched in November 2023, which compresses the settlement cycle from pricing to listing from T+5 to T+2, significantly reducing market and credit risk during the offering period. Issuers, sponsors, receiving banks, registrars and HKSCC all coordinate through the platform. A longer-term change is the migration of the cash market as a whole to T+1: HKEX published its consultation conclusions in October 2026, targeting implementation in the second half of 2028, subject to market readiness and regulatory approval. The direct implication for IPO projects is that launch execution and settlement processes will be compressed again, and issuers and intermediaries need to adjust their internal processes in advance. 9. Review Focus and Common Issues SEHK and SFC enquiries are not random; the vast majority fall into the following categories. Preparing in advance can significantly reduce the number of enquiry rounds. 9.1 Business and Suitability Business substance: revenue recognition policies, customer and supplier concentration, abnormal gross margins, related-party transactions, and consistency between fund flows and contracts. Sustainability: industry cycles, policy dependence, risk of losing major customers, sources of core technology and ownership of intellectual property. Suitability: management integrity, historical equity defects, administrative penalties, controlling shareholder background; SEHK may reject an application on the ground of “unsuitability for listing”. 9.2 Structure and Independence Competing business: where a controlling shareholder operates a competing business, disclosure must be made under Rule 8.10 of the reasons for exclusion, the scale of the competing business and evidence of independence. Connected transactions: continuing connected transactions after listing must comply with Chapter 14A; unnecessary related-party dealings must be eliminated before listing. VIE structure: validity of the contractual arrangements, compliance with foreign exchange and foreign investment access rules, and adequacy of risk disclosure. 9.3 Financials and Internal Controls Reporting accountant’s report: three financial years on the Main Board and two on GEM; the latest financial period must not be more than 6 months before the listing document. Internal controls: the degree to which processes such as treasury management, procurement and sales, inventory and approval of connected transactions are institutionalised; internal control adviser reports are often required. Tax and social security: historical underpayments, reliance on tax incentives and transfer pricing on cross-border transactions. 9.4 Offering and Public Float Public float and free float: the market-cap-tiered public float percentage, 300 shareholders, the 50% cap on the top three public shareholders and the free float threshold—failure on any one of these prevents listing. Independence of cornerstones and the underwriting syndicate: independence of cornerstone investors, source of subscription funds and whether any side agreements exist. Pre-IPO investment: fairness of the entry price, whether special rights have been terminated, and whether the investment amounts to last-minute pre-IPO shareholding. 9.5 The Most Common “Blockers” Table 12 High-Frequency Blockers and Responses Blocker Consequence Response A1 documents not “substantially complete” Application returned; 8-week wait before resubmission Sponsor performs a completeness check before submission; all main sections of the listing document in place Not completed within 6 months Application lapses, fee not refunded, resubmission required Work back from the deadline; schedule a stub-period audit before the financial information expires Insufficient public float/free float Listing conditions cannot be met Design the offering size and secondary share sale in advance; model each tier Competing business/connected transactions not cleaned up Repeated enquiries, hearing delays Resolve during restructuring; avoid filing a defective application Questionable earnings quality More enquiry rounds, valuation pressure Standardise revenue recognition; prepare customer and fund-flow verification working papers Note: The above summarises practical experience and does not represent a regulatory position. 10. Rule Changes in 2025–2026 New public float and free float framework (effective 4 August 2025): the flat 25% requirement was replaced by market-cap tiers (25%/15%/10%), and a free float requirement was introduced (≥10% and market cap ≥ HK$50 million, or market cap ≥ HK$600 million). This is more flexible for large issuers but places greater emphasis on genuinely tradable shares for small and medium-sized issuers. Optional publication of the Application Proof: the current Rule 12.01A is framed as “if the applicant elects to publish”; where the applicant elects to publish, the AP must be submitted on the same day as the A1. Applicants that do not elect to publish must still publish a PHIP after the hearing. Chapter 18C market cap and revenue thresholds: commercialised Specialist Technology companies—market cap at listing of not less than HK$6 billion and Specialist Technology revenue of not less than HK$250 million in the most recent audited year; pre-commercial companies—market cap of not less than HK$10 billion, with no revenue requirement. FINI enhancements: a round of functional upgrades in 2025 further reduced manual steps in launch execution. T+1 consultation conclusions (October 2026): the cash market targets T+1 implementation in the second half of 2028, subject to market readiness and regulatory approval; T+2 remains in place for now. 11. Practical Recommendations Treat sponsor appointment as the T-2 starting point: because of the statutory 2-month interval, the later the sponsor is in place, the later the A1 is filed; start sponsor selection as soon as the restructuring plan has largely taken shape. Fix “hard defects” before discussing valuation: competing business, connected transactions, equity defects and missing licences are structural issues; leaving them to the enquiry stage often leads to hearing delays or even withdrawal. Front-load audit and internal controls: the three-year (or two-year) financial statements and internal control remediation sit on the longest critical path and should run in parallel with, not after, restructuring. Plan backwards from the 6-month validity period: convert enquiry rounds, stub-period audits, hearing scheduling and the market window into weeks, and build in a buffer of at least 4–6 weeks. Enquiry responses should be “complete” rather than “fast”: the rules expressly prohibit fragmented revisions; each version of the listing document should address all comments in one go, otherwise a redo may be required. Design the offering structure and public float together: offering size, secondary share sales, cornerstone allocation and the clawback mechanism jointly determine whether the public float and free float thresholds are met, and should be modelled before submission. Watch the market window: passing review does not guarantee a successful launch; pricing and demand depend on the window, and where necessary it is better to delay the offering than to price reluctantly. The Way of Heaven and the Way of Man: The Ancient Wisdom Behind the Wealth Gap

Note: This is my original note and commentary based on episode 7 of the AI Historical Anecdotes series by the Douyin account “Who Moved My History”. It is not a verbatim transcript. The original video was published on 2026-09-03, and the creator states the content is AI-generated. Original video: v.douyin.com/6XIgWJ9wKLM The video is framed as a dialogue with Laozi and uses the Daodejing’s line “The Way of Heaven reduces the surplus to supplement the deficient; the Way of Man does the opposite, taking from the deficient to serve the surplus” as its thesis. It explains the operating rules behind the wealth gap and offers a methodology for ordinary people to break through. I. The Core Proposition: One Sentence That Reveals the Law of the World The Way of Heaven reduces the surplus to supplement the deficient; The Way of Man is different: it takes from the deficient to serve the surplus. — Daodejing This sentence reveals two layers of rules: The Way of Heaven (natural law) The Way of Man (social law) Direction Reduce the surplus, supplement the deficient (take from the rich to help the poor; maintain balance) Take from the deficient, serve the surplus (take from the poor to enrich the rich; the strong get stronger) Goal Seek balance; no single power may dominate Reward the strong; devour the weak Analogy Eagles breed slowly, sparrows breed quickly; the top is capped Snowballing; the Matthew Effect A natural person asks: Why does the Way of Heaven support the weak, while the Way of Man robs the poor to enrich the rich? II. Why Does the Way of Heaven “Cut Peaks and Fill Valleys”? — Nature’s Invisible Hand Use ecological niches as an analogy: a sparrow lays five or six eggs per clutch and has two or three clutches a year; an eagle lays only one or two eggs a year, and its chicks have a high mortality rate. If eagles also bred wildly and all their chicks survived, they would eat all their prey and eventually go extinct themselves. → This is “reducing the surplus to supplement the deficient”: nature firmly caps the reproductive lifeline of apex predators in order to preserve life at the bottom. Conclusion: The Way of Heaven does not allow one power to dominate or a winner to take all. III. Why Does the Way of Man Work in Reverse? — “Social Consensus” and the Matthew Effect The Way of Man works in the opposite direction because human society has built a system of “social consensus”. The modern scholar Robert K. Merton coined the term “Matthew Effect” for the same phenomenon, and it is the core of the Way of Man: For to everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. An academic example: the same paper — with a giant’s name attached → causes a sensation; with an unknown author’s name attached → gathers dust in a pile of papers. Fame automatically mints more fame; capital automatically breeds more capital. A coffee shop example: two coffee shops open on the same street at the same time — the one on the left hangs a well-known chain’s sign: headquarters handles site selection and the supply chain, and people come on day one because of the brand; the one on the right is run by a young independent owner. The coffee is just as good, but few people walk in during the first month. The reason: the left one has endorsement and backing, so customers do not have to take a risk; the right one may be better, but nobody knows about it. The cruelty of the Way of Man is this: it only looks at whether you have initial chips in your hand. For the same mistake, someone with chips gets a scratch; someone without chips is out of the game. The gap widens bit by bit. In the end it looks like a gap in ability, but from the very beginning it was a gap in chips. “The system itself rewards the strong and devours the weak.” IV. Can the Rules of the Way of Man Be Broken? — You Cannot Escape the Circle Drawn by the Way of Heaven Man follows the earth, the earth follows heaven, heaven follows the Way, and the Way follows nature. No matter how much the Way of Man jumps around, it cannot escape the circle drawn by the Way of Heaven. When something that once flourished reaches a critical point, the balancing mechanism of the Way of Heaven kicks in: the too-strong are weakened, the too-concentrated are dispersed. But the key is: that critical point will not come looking for you. You have to create the conditions yourself and make it tilt in your direction. A Methodology for Breaking Through (Step by Step) Step 1 | Let go of emotions Many people, once they see the nature of “the rich getting richer”, become cynical. But emotion is the cheapest thing there is; it traps you in a dead end. Analogy: when a strong wind hits at sea, cursing the sky will not move the boat. A real sailor shuts up immediately, watches the wind, and adjusts the sails. → Acknowledge that the system exists, treat it as objective terrain, and then look for leverage. Step 2 | First “have” a snowball, rather than “roll” one The Way of Man is like snowballing: if you already have a snowball, one push makes it bigger; if you do not, the most important thing is not to find a steep slope but to first pack a ball of snow. The essence of being “deficient” = not yet having an initial snowball (no resources, no endorsement). → The urgent question is not “how to roll” but “how to first have something”. Step 3 | Let people see you first You have done a lot of work but nobody sees it? That is the biggest problem. You must first make people notice you; only then will they come near you and give you resources. Do not believe that “gold will always shine”. If you do not show it, nobody knows what you are made of. Let people see you first. Step 4 | One word: “good” — be patient and accumulate Most people do not lose at the starting line; they lose to impatience: they act blindly when provoked and lie flat when frustrated. People who truly gain a foothold are those who quietly accumulate strength for a long time in a corner where nobody is watching. The bamboo analogy: it can shoot up because its roots have accumulated nutrients across hundreds of square meters underground. The roots go deep. Step 5 | The highest good is like water: work with a high profile, live with a low profile After accumulating resources, you must remember another line: the highest good is like water — water nourishes all things yet always stays in the lowest place. If you show your edge and sit high above others, the Way of Heaven will immediately suppress you. A good line: work with a high profile, but live with a low profile. Showing is necessary, but “what to show, how much to show, and when to show” matters: Let others see that you are doing things, but do not let them see through what you are thinking. Put your abilities on the table; keep your thoughts in your belly. V. For Managers: Plant Seeds of the Way of Heaven Within the Framework of the Way of Man Teams also follow the Way of Man: high performers get more resources, while average performers are gradually pushed out. If left alone, the team will inevitably end up with a few people holding all the opportunities while the rest coast, and efficiency will decline. A good manager must plant seeds of the Way of Heaven within the framework of the Way of Man: when a big tree blocks all the sunlight, as the person who sets the rules, you must cut away the excess branches; bind the interests of the strong to the growth of newcomers; assign people who compete for credit to different projects so they compete separately; when the system is about to monopolize, you must be the “heaven” that starts “reducing the surplus to supplement the deficient”. VI. Conclusion: Understand and Use Both the Way of Heaven and the Way of Man The Way of Heaven gives me awe and balance; the Way of Man forces me to show and accumulate. A low starting point is not frightening. What is frightening is being kidnapped by anger and refusing to think about how to make the rules work for you. The Way of Heaven and the Way of Man are not a choice between two; you must understand and use both at the same time — the Way of Heaven gives you the bottom line and the direction; the Way of Man gives you the methods and the path. If you want to change, the best time is to start right now.

I wanted to access and control the Kubernetes API using certificates. I looked around online but did not find a single good write-up, so I collected a few articles and put them together. It is a bit messy, but the general idea is clear. Feel free to take what is useful. API Server kube-apiserver is one of the most important core components of Kubernetes. Its main responsibilities are: Providing the REST API for cluster management, including authentication, authorization, data validation, and cluster state changes Acting as the hub for data exchange and communication between other modules (other modules query or modify data through the API Server; only the API Server directly operates on etcd) REST API kube-apiserver can serve both HTTPS (listening on port 6443 by default) and HTTP (listening on 127.0.0.1:8080 by default). The HTTP API is insecure and performs no authentication or authorization; do not enable it in production. Both endpoints expose the same REST API format. See the Kubernetes API Reference for the call format of every API. Local port Receives HTTP requests Defaults to 8080; change it with the API Server’s startup flag Defaults to the IP; change it with the startup flag Unauthenticated and unauthorized HTTP requests reach the API Server through this port Secure port Defaults to 6443; change it with the startup flag The default IP is a non-local host network address; set it with the startup flag Receives HTTPS requests Used for authentication based on token files, client certificates, and HTTP Basic auth Used for policy-based authorization HTTPS access control is not enabled by default Open a local unauthenticated debug port: Examples: Node-related endpoints The REST path for Node-related endpoints is , where is the node name or IP address. The Pod information obtained here comes from the Node rather than the etcd database, so the two may differ in time. Generate the server key and certificate, and sign them with the CA certificate 3. Generate the client key and certificate, and sign them with the CA certificate 4. Create the SSL secret 5. curl calling example Extra: Grant a ClusterRole to a user For a typical application, the user provides a username and password, the server checks the database to see whether they exist and are valid, and authentication succeeds or fails accordingly. How does Kubernetes do it? Although ordinary users cannot be created through API calls, Kubernetes cleverly authenticates users via certificates. In other words, any user who can present a valid certificate is authenticated by Kubernetes. After authentication, Kubernetes treats the certificate’s CN as the username (for example, means the username is ) and the Organization as the user’s group. A Role bound to that username and group then determines the user’s permissions.

DynamoDB Basic Concepts Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL database service that provides fast, predictable performance and seamless scalability. Basic structure DynamoDB has a few core concepts: tables, items, and attributes. A table is a collection of items, and each item is a collection of attributes. You can think of them as the equivalent of collections, documents, and fields in MongoDB. Primary keys in DynamoDB Unlike MongoDB, DynamoDB does not generate an by default to uniquely identify a record. That is why DynamoDB has the concept of a primary key. You specify the primary key of a table, and the primary key uniquely identifies each item in the table (by designating one attribute as the primary key). DynamoDB supports two kinds of primary keys: 1. Partition key DynamoDB uses the value of the partition key as the input to an internal hash function. The output of the hash function determines the partition where the item is stored (the physical storage inside DynamoDB). 2. Composite primary key (partition key and sort key) DynamoDB uses the partition key value as the input to an internal hash function. The output of the hash function determines the partition where the item is stored (the physical storage inside DynamoDB). All items with the same partition key are stored together, sorted by the sort key value. In a table with a partition key and a sort key, two items may have the same partition key value, but they must have different sort key values.
